questions.question: List two key advantages of capacitive touchscreens over resistive touchscreens.
questions.solution_html:
• List two key advantages of capacitive touchscreens over resistive touchscreens.
  • Multi-touch support: Capacitive screens can recognize multiple touches simultaneously
  • such as pinch-to-zoom gestures.
  • Use large text, buttons, and clear icons to improve readability and ease of interaction.
  • User frustration: Long delays make users impatient and dissatisfied.
  • Speaker positioning: Each participant's voice appears to come from a different virtual
  • location.
  • Set a reasonable timeout for each network request.
  • Mental demand: Amount of thinking and concentration required.
  • Request to speak: A participant clicks the Raise Hand button.
  • Disable dates that are in the past when selecting a future flight.
  • Require essential fields such as origin, destination, and departure date.
  • Information architecture
  • Information architecture (IA) refers to the systematic organization, classification, and
  • presentation of information within an application.
  • a) Content categorization
  • Social media platforms organize content into categories such as posts, reels, videos, stories
  • messages, groups, and notifications. Proper categorization helps users understand where
  • information is located.
  • b) Hierarchical organization
  • Important features are placed prominently, while secondary features are organized within menus
  • or submenus. For example, the home feed is usually more prominent than settings.
  • c) Search and filtering
  • Search bars, hashtags, keywords, and filters allow users to locate specific people, posts, videos
  • and topics.
  • d) Personalized content organization
  • Algorithms recommend posts based on users' interests, viewing history, and interactions.
  • Personalization can improve content relevance, but it can also create repetitive content and filter
  • bubbles.
  • e) Consistency
  • Consistent labels, icons, and layouts across different screens help users learn the interface more
  • easily.
  • Ease of use: Clear categories and navigation reduce the effort required to find content.
  • Visual hierarchy: Use headings, spacing, size, and contrast to distinguish important
  • information.
  • Affordances
  • Affordances are the possible actions that an object or interface allows a user to perform.
  • In a kitchen appliance control panel, different controls should support the actions expected of
  • them.
  • Implementation
  •  A physical knob affords turning.
  •  A raised button affords pressing.
  •  A touchscreen slider affords dragging.
  •  A door handle affords pulling.
  •  A Start button affords initiating a cooking operation.
  • Each control should have a shape and behaviour appropriate to its function. For example, a
  • rotary knob is suitable for adjusting temperature or cooking time because it allows continuous
  • adjustment.
  • Example: A large rotary knob can be used to set cooking time, while a clearly pressable button
  • starts the operation.
  • Good affordances reduce the need for lengthy instructions and make the appliance easier to
  • learn.
  • Display the selected cooking mode and temperature.
  • The user identifies the Microwave button through its signifier.
  • System architecture
  • The architecture of an AR surgical training system consists of several connected components.
  • User and physical environment
  • Surgeon, student, mannequin, physical instruments
  • Sensing and tracking layer
  • Cameras, depth sensors, hand tracking, instrument tracking
  • AR processing and registration layer
  • Spatial mapping, coordinate transformation, pose estimation
  • Anatomical and simulation engine
  • 3D models, tissue properties, surgical simulation, assessment
  • Rendering and interaction layer
  • 3D visualization, menus, labels, gestures, voice, feedback
  • AR display and user feedback
  • Head-mounted display, spatial overlays, visual and audio feedback
  • The system operates as a continuous loop. The sensors detect user movement, the processing
  • layer updates the position of virtual objects, and the rendering layer displays the updated scene.
  • Guided training: Step-by-step instructions demonstrate the correct sequence of actions.

questions.question: Summarize the primary limitation of predictive cognitive models.
questions.solution_html:
• Better sensitivity and clarity: They respond to light finger touches and generally provide
  • better screen clarity because they do not require pressure-sensitive layers.
  • Summarize the primary limitation of predictive cognitive models.
  • The primary limitation of predictive cognitive models is that they assume users behave in a
  • predictable and consistent manner. They may not accurately represent differences in experience
  • emotions, distractions, learning, and real-world situations.
  • Provide simple navigation, high colour contrast, clear feedback, and sufficient time to
  • complete tasks.
  • Loss of concentration: Users may forget their previous actions or lose focus while
  • waiting.
  • Improved identification: Users can identify who is speaking based on the apparent
  • direction of the voice.
  • Display a message such as “Network timeout. Please try again.”
  • Physical demand: Physical effort needed to complete the task.
  • Queue management: The system places the participant in a speaking queue.
  • Prevent the return date from being earlier than the departure date.
  • Prevent users from selecting the same airport as both origin and destination, where
  • inappropriate.
  • Navigation paradigms
  • Navigation paradigms define how users move between sections and access information.
  • a) Tab-based navigation
  • A bottom or top navigation bar provides access to important sections, such as Home, Search
  • Reels, Notifications, and Profile.
  • b) Feed-based navigation
  • Users scroll vertically through a continuous stream of content. Infinite scrolling reduces
  • interruptions but may encourage excessive use.
  • c) Search-based navigation
  • Users enter keywords, names, or hashtags to locate specific content directly.
  • d) Hierarchical navigation
  • Users move through levels such as Home → Groups → Group Details → Posts. Breadcrumbs or
  • back buttons can help users understand their location.
  • e) Notification-based navigation
  • Notifications provide direct links to comments, likes, messages, and other activities. They help
  • users return to relevant content but can also interrupt ongoing tasks.
  • Increased participation: Likes, comments, shares, and messaging make interaction easy.
  • Progressive disclosure: Display essential information first and reveal advanced options
  • only when required.
  • Signifiers
  • Signifiers are visible or perceivable indicators that communicate where and how an action should
  • be performed. An affordance describes a possible action, whereas a signifier helps the user
  • discover that action.
  • Implementation
  •  Label buttons as Start, Stop, Timer, and Temperature.
  •  Use recognizable symbols for microwave, grill, defrost, and fan functions.
  •  Provide arrows around rotary knobs to indicate the direction of adjustment.
  •  Use contrasting colours to distinguish important controls.
  •  Display units such as °C, minutes, and seconds beside the corresponding values.
  • Example: A snowflake symbol accompanied by the label “Defrost” helps users identify the
  • defrosting function.
  • Labels should be clear and consistent. Designers should not rely exclusively on colour or
  • unfamiliar icons because users may have different levels of experience or visual ability.
  • Show a countdown timer during operation.
  • The button affords pressing, providing an affordance.
  • Anatomical data and 3D modelling
  • The system uses medical imaging data, such as CT scans and MRI scans, to construct three
  • dimensional anatomical models.
  • Important features include
  •  Three-dimensional representations of organs, bones, muscles, nerves, and blood vessels.
  •  Separate anatomical layers that can be shown or hidden.
  •  Colour coding to distinguish different structures.
  •  Labels and annotations identifying anatomical parts.
  •  Models that support rotation, zooming, slicing, and cross-sectional views.
  • Example: A medical student can view a 3D heart model, rotate it, and examine its chambers and
  • blood vessels from different angles.
  • The anatomical models should be reviewed by qualified medical professionals to ensure
  • educational accuracy.
  • Anatomical exploration: Students inspect the location and relationship of anatomical
  • structures.

questions.question: Define cart abandonment in e-commerce interaction design.
questions.solution_html:
• Cart abandonment occurs when a customer adds products to an online shopping cart but leaves
  • the website without completing the purchase.
  • Example: A customer adds a mobile phone to the cart but leaves after seeing unexpected delivery
  • charges.
  • Reduced productivity: Slow systems increase task completion time and reduce efficiency.
  • Reduced confusion: Separating speakers spatially makes overlapping conversations easier
  • to follow.
  • Provide Retry and Cancel buttons.
  • Temporal demand: Pressure caused by time limitations.
  • Grant permission: The host or system grants the speaking floor to the next participant.
  • Highlight valid dates and clearly distinguish unavailable dates.
  • Restrict passenger numbers to supported limits.
  • Interaction design patterns
  • Interaction design patterns are reusable solutions to common interface problems.
  • a) Like, comment, and share
  • These familiar controls make interaction simple and encourage users to participate in
  • discussions.
  • b) Follow and subscribe
  • Users can receive updates from people, creators, or channels they find interesting.
  • c) Infinite scrolling
  • New content loads automatically as users move down the feed. This reduces navigation effort but
  • can make it difficult to stop browsing.
  • d) Pull-to-refresh
  • Users can refresh a feed through a simple gesture to view updated content.
  • e) Notifications and feedback
  • Badges, animations, sound alerts, and confirmation messages communicate the result of user
  • actions.
  • f) Personalization
  • Recommendation systems present content based on user interests and previous behaviour
  • increasing the likelihood of relevant engagement.
  • Personal relevance: Recommendations help users discover content related to their
  • interests.
  • Notification control: Allow users to disable, group, or schedule notifications.
  • Mapping
  • Mapping refers to the relationship between a control and the result it produces. Good mapping
  • makes the relationship between the user's action and the appliance's response easy to understand.
  • Implementation
  •  Arrange temperature controls near the temperature display.
  •  Place timer controls close to the cooking-time display.
  •  Use a clockwise knob movement to increase time and an anticlockwise movement to
  • decrease it, with clear directional indicators.
  •  Arrange temperature values in increasing order.
  •  Place Start and Stop controls in predictable locations.
  • Example: If a user turns a temperature knob clockwise, the displayed temperature should
  • increase. If the user turns it anticlockwise, the temperature should decrease.
  • Poor mapping can cause errors. For example, placing the temperature and timer controls far apart
  • from their displays may confuse users about which setting they are changing.
  • Provide a sound or visual signal when cooking finishes.
  • The user selects a power level and turns the time knob; the controls have clear mapping
  • to the displayed settings.
  • Spatial user interface design
  • A spatial user interface places virtual controls and information within the user's three
  • dimensional environment rather than limiting the interface to a flat screen.
  • a) Spatial anchoring
  • Virtual anatomical structures should remain aligned with the physical mannequin or training
  • model as the user moves.
  • b) Depth and positioning
  • Important structures should appear at appropriate distances and depths to support accurate
  • perception.
  • c) Direct manipulation
  • Users should be able to select, rotate, enlarge, or isolate anatomical structures using natural
  • gestures or tracked tools.
  • d) Contextual menus
  • Controls should appear near the relevant anatomical structure when useful, without blocking the
  • user's view.
  • e) Layer management
  • Users should be able to reveal or hide structures such as skin, muscles, bones, and organs.
  • f) Visual hierarchy
  • Important structures should be highlighted without overwhelming the user with labels
  • animations, or unrelated information.
  • Instrument simulation: The system tracks virtual or physical instruments.

questions.question: Define Ubiquitous Computing (Ubicomp) as envisioned by Mark Weiser.
questions.solution_html:
• Ubiquitous computing, proposed by Mark Weiser, is the concept of embedding computers into
  • everyday objects and environments so that computing becomes available everywhere and
  • operates unobtrusively in the background.
  • Example: Smart lights that automatically adjust according to room conditions.
  • Repeated actions: Users may click buttons repeatedly, assuming the system has not
  • received their input.
  • Natural conversation: Virtual meetings become more similar to face-to-face meetings.
  • Limit automatic retries and use increasing delays between attempts.
  • Performance: How successful the user feels they were.
  • Enable microphone: The participant's microphone is enabled, subject to their device and
  • permissions.
  • Use calendar controls instead of requiring users to type dates manually.
  • Show a booking summary before payment.
  • Impact on user engagement
  • Effective information architecture and interaction patterns improve user engagement in several
  • ways
  • Social connection: Notifications and messaging support communication with friends and
  • communities.
  • Clear navigation: Use familiar labels, consistent icons, and a manageable number of
  • menu options.
  • Feedback
  • Feedback communicates the result of a user's action. It confirms whether the system has received
  • and processed an instruction.
  • Implementation
  • Illuminate the selected function.
  • The screen immediately displays the selected power and cooking time, providing
  • feedback.
  • Interaction techniques
  • The system should support multiple interaction methods to suit different training activities.
  • Hand gestures: Pinching can select a structure, while dragging can rotate or reposition a virtual
  • model.
  • Voice commands: Commands such as “Show the heart” or “Hide muscles” allow hands-free
  • interaction.
  • Gaze interaction: Looking at a structure can highlight it or prepare it for selection.
  • Instrument tracking: Specially tracked surgical instruments can interact with virtual tissues in the
  • training environment.
  • Touch interaction: A connected tablet or control panel can be used to select procedures, change
  • settings, or review instructions.
  • For safety and accuracy, the system should provide clear confirmation when an important action
  • is performed and prevent accidental changes during a training task.
  • Procedure guidance: Visual indicators identify the target area and important structures.
questions.final_answer: Procedure guidance: Visual indicators identify the target area and important structures

questions.question: List two interface design adaptations specifically needed for elderly users.
questions.solution_html:
• List two interface design adaptations specifically needed for elderly users.
  • Reduced trust: Frequent delays make users believe the system is unreliable.
  • Design solutions
  •  Display a progress indicator during lengthy operations.
  •  Provide immediate feedback after every action.
  •  Optimize the system to reduce unnecessary delays.
  •  Show timeout messages and retry options when appropriate.
  • Conclusion: Fast and predictable responses improve user performance, confidence, and
  • satisfaction.
  • Adjustable audio: Users can adjust the volume or position of individual speakers when
  • supported.
  • Example: In a virtual seminar, the presenter may appear in front, while participants are
  • positioned around a virtual table.
  • Conclusion: Spatial audio improves speaker identification, reduces listening effort, and supports
  • clearer communication in virtual meeting rooms.
  • Prevent duplicate transactions by using idempotency keys or checking the operation
  • status before retrying payments.
  • Conclusion: Proper timeout and retry handling improves reliability and prevents user confusion
  • and duplicate operations.
  • Effort: Amount of mental and physical effort required.
  • Release the floor: After speaking, the participant clicks Done or the host revokes
  • speaking permission.
  • Validate the selected dates before allowing the user to proceed.
  • Applications in a flight booking form
  • Ask for confirmation before completing a payment or cancelling a booking.
  • Example: If a user selects 20 December as the departure date, the system should prevent them
  • from selecting 15 December as the return date.
  • Conclusion: Error prevention reduces booking mistakes, improves usability, and saves users time
  • and money.
  • User retention: Consistent design and useful features encourage users to return to the
  • platform.
  • However, engagement should not be measured only by the amount of time users spend on a
  • platform. Meaningful interaction, satisfaction, accessibility, and user control are also important.
  • Cognitive overload
  • Cognitive overload occurs when the amount of information or number of decisions exceeds the
  • user's available mental processing capacity.
  • Social media can cause cognitive overload through
  •  Excessive notifications and interruptions.
  •  Large quantities of rapidly changing content.
  •  Too many choices and competing visual elements.
  •  Repeated recommendations and advertisements.
  •  Frequent switching between messages, feeds, and videos.
  •  Infinite scrolling that makes it difficult to estimate how much content remains.
  • These factors can reduce concentration, increase mental fatigue, and make important information
  • difficult to remember.
  • User control: Provide controls for recommendation preferences, feed settings, and
  • autoplay.
  • Display an error message if the door is open or a setting is invalid.
  • Constraints
  • Constraints limit the actions a user can perform to prevent mistakes and unsafe operation.
  • Implementation
  •  Prevent operation when the door is open.
  •  Restrict temperature settings to supported values.
  •  Prevent negative cooking times.
  •  Disable incompatible functions when another mode is selected.
  •  Require confirmation before cancelling a long cooking cycle when appropriate.
  •  Provide a child lock to prevent accidental operation.
  • Example: If the user tries to start a microwave while the door is open, the appliance should
  • refuse to start and display “Please close the door.”
  • Constraints can be physical, logical, semantic, or cultural. Physical constraints prevent actions
  • through the structure of the device, while logical constraints prevent invalid combinations of
  • settings.
  • If the door is open or the selected value is invalid, constraints prevent the operation.
  • Surgical simulation and training
  • A surgical training module allows students to practise selected procedures in a simulated
  • environment.
  • The system may include
  • Error detection: The system identifies deviations from the predefined training procedure.
questions.final_answer: Error detection: The system identifies deviations from the predefined training procedure

questions.question: Discuss the psychological impact of system response time and delay on user performance.
questions.solution_html:
• performance.
  • System response time is the time taken by a computer system to respond to a user's action.
  • Response time and delay affect user satisfaction, concentration, efficiency, and confidence.
  • Frustration: Feelings of stress, irritation, or insecurity.
  • Procedure
  •  Ask participants to perform a specified task on the interactive system.
  •  After completing the task, ask them to rate each dimension, commonly on a scale from 0
  • to 100.
  •  In the traditional NASA-TLX procedure, participants also make pairwise comparisons to
  • assign relative weights to the dimensions.
  •  Calculate the overall weighted workload score.
  •  Compare scores across users, tasks, or interface designs.
  • Example: If users report high mental demand and frustration while completing an online booking
  • form, the designer can simplify the form and reduce unnecessary steps.
  • Conclusion: NASA-TLX helps designers identify demanding tasks and improve usability.
  • Next speaker: The system grants the floor to the next person in the queue.
  • Additional features
  •  Display the current speaker's name.
  •  Notify participants when their turn arrives.
  •  Allow the host to interrupt or remove disruptive speakers.
  •  Give priority to the moderator for emergencies.
  •  Prevent two participants from receiving exclusive floor control simultaneously.
  • Conclusion: A well-designed floor control protocol reduces interruptions, promotes fairness, and
  • makes online seminars easier to manage.
  • Design solutions to reduce cognitive overload
  • Designers can reduce cognitive overload by applying the following principles
  • Accessibility: Support readable text, sufficient contrast, screen readers, and keyboard
  • navigation.
  • Show a clear confirmation when a setting is saved.
  • Example: When the user presses Start, the display should show the remaining cooking time and
  • indicate that cooking has begun.
  • Feedback should be immediate, clear, and appropriate. Important warnings must be
  • distinguishable from ordinary status messages.
  • Systematic integration of the principles
  • These principles should work together rather than independently.
  • Consider the process of heating food
  • After the user presses Start, the countdown display and completion alarm communicate
  • the progress and result.
  • Performance evaluation: The system records task completion time, movement accuracy
  • and procedural errors.
  • For example, during a simulated procedure, the system can highlight a target anatomical region
  • and warn the trainee when a tracked instrument approaches a designated structure that should be
  • avoided.
  • Such feedback must be based on validated training rules rather than being presented as an
  • authoritative clinical decision.
  • Feedback and error prevention
  • Feedback is important because users need to understand how their actions affect the virtual
  • environment.
  • The system can provide
  •  Visual highlights when an anatomical structure is selected.
  •  Labels confirming the selected organ.
  •  Audio notifications for important training events.
  •  Progress indicators showing the current training stage.
  •  Warnings when the user deviates from a simulated procedure.
  •  A reset option to restore the initial training state.
  • Error-prevention mechanisms should include confirmation for resetting a session, protection
  • against accidental deletion of progress, and clear instructions when tracking is lost.
  • The system should never silently display inaccurate spatial alignment. If tracking becomes
  • unreliable, it should clearly notify the user and suspend any affected precision-dependent
  • training task.

questions.question: Compare remote asynchronous usability testing with moderated in- / person usability testing.
questions.solution_html:
• Compare remote asynchronous usability testing with moderated in-person
  • usability testing.
  • Usability testing evaluates how easily users can interact with a system.
  • Remote asynchronous testing Moderated in-person testing
  • Participants complete tasks remotely at Participants complete tasks under the guidance of a
  • their convenience. moderator.
  • No moderator is present during the session. A moderator observes and guides the session.
  • Less expensive and easier to conduct with
  • More expensive and requires scheduling.
  • many users.
  • Suitable for geographically distributed Usually conducted in a laboratory or a common
  • participants. location.
  • Limited opportunity to ask follow-up The moderator can ask questions and clarify user
  • questions immediately. behaviour.
  • Useful for measuring task completion rates Useful for understanding user emotions, confusion
  • and time. and thought processes.
  • Conclusion: Remote asynchronous testing is suitable for large-scale testing at low cost, whereas
  • moderated in-person testing provides deeper insights into user behaviour.
  • Meaningful feedback: Communicate successful actions without unnecessary animations
  • or interruptions.
  • Additional design considerations
  • Consistency: Similar controls should behave similarly across different operating modes.
  • Error prevention: Provide reasonable defaults and prevent incompatible settings.
  • Accessibility: Use large buttons, readable text, high contrast, and tactile controls where
  • appropriate.
  • Safety: Separate dangerous or irreversible operations from ordinary controls, and provide clear
  • warnings.
  • Simplicity: Group related functions together and avoid unnecessary controls.
  • Usability testing: Ask representative users to perform common tasks, such as defrosting food or
  • setting a timer. Observe errors, task completion time, and user satisfaction, then improve the
  • design.
  • Usability, accessibility, and safety
  • The system should be designed to reduce fatigue and mental workload.
  • Usability: Keep frequently used controls accessible and provide a consistent interaction pattern.
  • Accessibility: Support readable labels, sufficient contrast, adjustable text sizes, and alternatives
  • to gesture-based interaction.
  • Comfort: Reduce unnecessary visual movement and provide options to adjust the viewing
  • arrangement.
  • Safety: Distinguish simulated information from real patient data and prevent users from
  • confusing educational overlays with validated clinical guidance.
  • Privacy: Protect medical images and any personal information used during training.
  • Performance: Maintain low interaction latency and reliable tracking so that virtual structures
  • remain aligned with the physical environment.
